title: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification

sections.title: Adaptations as Outcomes of Structural Change

slides.title: The Plant Kingdom
slides.kicker: Green factories that feed the planet
bullets: Plants are multicellular, autotrophic organisms: they make their own food through photosynthesis.
Their cells have a rigid cell wall made mainly of cellulose, which provides support and protection.
Plants form the base of most food chains and release the oxygen essential for life on the Earth.
slides.note: Every breath you take is a plant's gift!

slides.title: Five Classes of Plants
slides.kicker: One kingdom, five classes to explore
bullets: All plants belong to kingdom Plantae, which is further divided into five classes.
The classes are Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, Gymnosperm and Angiosperm.
Thallophytes are described as among the simplest plant forms, mostly found in water or moist environments.
slides.note: Five shelves in the green library of life.

slides.title: Thallophyta: Simple Aquatic Bodies
slides.kicker: Algae with simple thallus bodies
bullets: Thallophyta joins thallos, meaning undifferentiated body, with phyton, meaning plant.
Their body, the thallus, is so simple that gases, nutrients and water exchange directly with the surroundings.
Mostly found in water or moist places, they are well adapted to aquatic habitats.
Spirogyra is a familiar example of Thallophyta.
slides.note: A simple body is a perfect body, if your home is a pond.

slides.title: Bryophyta: Amphibians of Plants
slides.kicker: First steps on land, still tied to water
bullets: Bryophyta joins bryon, meaning moss, with phyton; mosses and liverworts mark a shift from water to land.
They grow as green mats on damp rocks, walls of old buildings and soil, especially during the monsoons.
Their bodies are more differentiated than thallophytes: rhizoids plus simple stem-like and leaf-like structures.
Because they still require water for reproduction, bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.
slides.note: Try Activity 12.6 with a hand lens and a dissecting microscope!

slides.title: Lichens: Alga Plus Fungus
slides.kicker: Two partners, one team
bullets: A lichen is a symbiotic, mutual association between an alga and a fungus living as one body.
The fungal partner provides protection, while the algal partner photosynthesises and provides food.
Some lichens are poisonous, so classifying and identifying them properly keeps their utilisation safe.
slides.note: Two partners, one body: nature's teamwork!

slides.title: What Makes an Animal
slides.kicker: Multicellular movers that hunt for food
bullets: Animals are multicellular and heterotrophic organisms: they depend on other organisms for their food.
Most animals show locomotion, rapid response to stimuli and coordinated behaviour.
These abilities let animals actively search for food, avoid predators and interact with their surroundings.
slides.note: Animals move to find food, plants stay and make it.

slides.title: The Notochord Divide
slides.kicker: One flexible rod splits the animal kingdom
bullets: A major criterion for classifying animals is the presence or absence of the notochord, a flexible rod-shaped structure.
Animals without a notochord are non-chordata (invertebrata); animals with one are chordata.
In some chordates the notochord is a precursor for the vertebral column, and chordata splits into protochordata and vertebrata.

slides.title: Porifera: The Pore-Bearers
slides.kicker: Simplest body plan, no tissues
bullets: Sponges have one of the simplest animal body plans: multicellular, but without organisation of tissues and organs.
Numerous pores let water flow through continuously, bringing food particles and oxygen to cells and carrying waste away.
Poriferans remain fixed in one place and are found in aquatic environments.
slides.note: Could a sponge survive on land? Think and answer!

slides.title: Cnidaria: Tissues and Tentacles
slides.kicker: Tentacles replace waiting on water currents
bullets: Hydra, jellyfish and corals are cnidarians showing a major change: tissue-level organisation of the body.
Specialised cells do specific jobs, such as tentacles that capture prey instead of waiting for water currents.
One single opening serves both food intake and waste removal, a body-plan limitation worth pondering.

slides.title: Platyhelminthes: Directional Movement
slides.kicker: Symmetry gives movement a direction
bullets: Flatworms, the Platyhelminthes, show organisational advancement through bilateral symmetry and directional movement.
Studying invertebrates traces how the animal body gradually changed, from simple structures to complex organ systems.
Each step brings advances in movement, feeding habits and control and coordination, along with exceptions and new challenges.

slides.title: Structure Shapes Survival
slides.kicker: Fins, feathers, fur: structure shapes survival
bullets: Fins and gills allow fish to move and breathe in water.
Feathers and hollow bones make flight possible in birds.
Fat storage in camels and thick fur in polar bears support survival under extreme conditions.
In mammals, mammary glands improve the survival of young ones.
slides.note: Body parts are survival tools shaped by environments.

slides.title: The Ladder of Classification
slides.kicker: From kingdom wide to species narrow
bullets: Classification follows a step-by-step order, starting from very broad groups and moving to smaller, specific ones.
At each lower level, organisms share more common features than at the level above.
The full ladder runs Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
Every lower group is a part of the group above it.

slides.title: Classification Works Like an Address
slides.kicker: Zoom in step by step, like an address
bullets: The hierarchy works like a house address, which helps us locate a place exactly.
It lets scientists identify, compare and study organisms accurately, and understand how they are related.
Fig. 12.17 shows such pyramids for a tiger and a pea plant, with kingdom at the top and species at the base.
slides.note: Kingdom se species tak: zoom in like an address!

slides.title: One Name for the World
slides.kicker: Bagh, puli, tiger, tigre: one universal name
bullets: A tiger is bagh in Hindi, puli in Tamil, tiger in English and tigre in French, so confusion may arise.
Binomial nomenclature, introduced by Carolus Linnaeus in the 18th century, gives every organism one universal name.
Each scientific name has two parts, written in Latin or a Latinised form.

slides.title: Genus Plus Species
slides.kicker: Two words that work worldwide
bullets: The first word is the genus: Panthera holds the roaring cats, tiger and lion, which have similar skull structure.
The second word is the species: a group of similar individuals capable of interbreeding and producing offsprings.
Together the two words form a unique scientific name used worldwide, like Mangifera indica for mango.

slides.title: Rules for Scientific Names
slides.kicker: Capitals, order and italics matter
bullets: Rule one: the name has two parts, genus and species.
Rule two: the genus name comes first with a capital letter, followed by the species name in small letters.
Rule three: in print the name is written in italics, and when handwritten it is underlined.

items: Italics in print, underline by hand

slides.title: Three Domains of Life
slides.kicker: DNA rewrites the story: three domains
bullets: The five kingdom system was more comprehensive than earlier systems, yet could not fully explain the diversity of life.
With better microscopes and genetic studies, scientists began comparing organisms at the DNA level.
Organisms with similar DNA are considered to have a common ancestry.
From genetic data, Carl Woese proposed the three domain system in 1977: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
slides.note: Microbes were hiding their diversity until DNA spoke.

slides.title: What Are Fossils?
slides.kicker: Life's diary written in stone
bullets: Fossils are preserved remains of plants and animals found in layers of rocks, sand and mud.
They act as natural records of life on the Earth.
Fossils help us understand how life has changed over millions of years.

slides.title: Layers Tell Life's Story
slides.kicker: Older layers simple, newer layers complex
bullets: Generally, older layers contain simpler organisms.
Newer layers show more complex forms.
Reading layer by layer is like reading a book from its first page to the last.
slides.note: Read the rocks like pages of a book.

slides.title: Fossil Finds in India
slides.kicker: Dinosaurs, early humans, ancient plants
bullets: From giant dinosaurs to early humans and ancient plants, some important fossils have been discovered in India.
Each fossil is evidence that connects today's diversity with the life of the past.
Such natural records make fossils key evidence for how life changed over millions of years.

slides.title: Every Species Has a Role
slides.kicker: Lose one thread, the web weakens
bullets: Each species, large or small, plays an important role in nature.
Plants produce food and oxygen; animals pollinate flowers and disperse seeds; microorganisms recycle nutrients.
When one species disappears, others that depend on it may decline in number and eventually also disappear.
slides.note: Nature runs on teamwork: no role is too small.

slides.title: Biodiversity Under Threat
slides.kicker: Four pressures squeezing life's variety
bullets: Human activities such as pollution, deforestation, the overuse of resources and climate change are reducing biodiversity.
Losing species weakens the natural roles that keep the living world working.
That is why identifying and classifying species correctly is the first step to protecting them.

slides.title: The Purple Frog Story
slides.kicker: A 2003 discovery hidden underground
bullets: The Purple Frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) from Kerala has a species name after the Sahyadri Hills.
It lives underground for most of the year and comes out only during the monsoon to breed.
It belongs to an ancient family of frogs, as understood from fossils.
Its discovery in 2003 highlighted the need for biodiversity conservation in the Western Ghats.
slides.note: Discovered in 2003: nature still surprises us!

slides.title: Phumdis and the Sangai
slides.kicker: Floating homes of the dancing deer
bullets: Phumdis are floating grasslands in the Loktak lake of Keibul Lamjo National Park, Manipur, a unique habitat of the world.
These floating beds of soil, a few centimetres to two metres thick, grow rooted vegetation in rich organic matter.
They are home to the endangered Sangai, the dancing deer endemic to Manipur.
The deer was declared extinct in 1951 and was rediscovered in 1953.
slides.note: A deer that dances on floating meadows!

slides.title: Meet Birbal Sahni
slides.kicker: The fossil pioneer of Lucknow
bullets: Birbal Sahni was an eminent scientist who studied fossil plants.
He founded the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP) in Lucknow, which continues his work even today.
His studies connected plants with their ancestors and showed that life on the Earth has a long, connected history.

flashcards.front: Which kingdom do all plants belong to?
flashcards.back: Kingdom Plantae. Plants are multicellular autotrophs that perform photosynthesis.

flashcards.front: What makes up the plant cell wall and what does it do?
flashcards.back: Cellulose, mainly. The rigid wall provides support and protection to plant cells.

flashcards.front: What does the word Thallophyta literally mean?
flashcards.back: Thallos means undifferentiated body and phyton means plant; the body is a simple thallus.

flashcards.front: Name one example of Thallophyta.
flashcards.back: Spirogyra, an aquatic alga with a simple thallus body.

flashcards.front: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
flashcards.back: They live on land but still require water for reproduction, so they bridge both worlds.

flashcards.front: In a lichen, which partner makes the food?
flashcards.back: The algal partner photosynthesises and provides food; the fungal partner provides protection.

flashcards.front: What is a notochord?
flashcards.back: A flexible, rod-shaped structure whose presence or absence is a major criterion for classifying animals.

flashcards.front: Name the two animal groups split by the notochord.
flashcards.back: Non-chordata (invertebrata) without a notochord and chordata with one.

flashcards.front: How does a sponge get food and oxygen?
flashcards.back: Water flowing through body pores carries food particles and oxygen to cells and removes waste.

flashcards.front: Name three cnidarians.
flashcards.back: Hydra, jellyfish and corals.

flashcards.front: List the seven ranks of classification in order.
flashcards.back: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

flashcards.front: Which features make flight possible in birds?
flashcards.back: Feathers and hollow bones are the structural features that make flight possible.

flashcards.front: What changes as you move to lower levels of classification?
flashcards.back: Organisms share more common features; each lower group is part of the group above it.

flashcards.front: Who introduced binomial nomenclature, and when?
flashcards.back: Carolus Linnaeus, in the 18th century.

flashcards.front: What are the two parts of a scientific name?
flashcards.back: The genus name first, with a capital letter, and the species name second, in lower case.

flashcards.front: How is a scientific name written in print and by hand?

flashcards.front: What does a species name indicate?
flashcards.back: A group of similar individuals capable of interbreeding and producing offsprings.

quiz.q: Plants are called autotrophic because they...
options: make their own food by photosynthesis
absorb ready-made food from other organisms
do not need any food at all
quiz.why: The book defines plants as multicellular autotrophs that perform photosynthesis.

quiz.q: The rigid plant cell wall is made primarily of...
quiz.why: Cellulose walls provide plant cells with support and protection.

quiz.q: A water plant with a simple, undifferentiated thallus body belongs to...
quiz.why: Thallophytes like Spirogyra have a simple thallus and live in water.

quiz.q: Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom because they...
options: live on land but need water to reproduce
are half animal and half plant
quiz.why: They colonised land yet remain dependent on water for reproduction.

quiz.q: In a lichen, which partner photosynthesises and provides food?
quiz.why: The fungus gives protection; the alga photosynthesises and provides food.

quiz.q: Animals are heterotrophic, which means they...
options: depend on other organisms for food
quiz.why: The book states animals depend on other organisms for their food.

quiz.q: The flexible, rod-shaped structure used to classify animals is the...
quiz.why: Presence or absence of the notochord is a major criterion for classifying animals.

quiz.q: Water flowing through a sponge's pores mainly...
options: brings food and oxygen to cells and carries waste away
helps the sponge swim to new places
quiz.why: Pores let water carry food particles and oxygen in and waste out.

quiz.q: A limitation of the cnidarian body plan is that...
options: they have no cells at all
one opening serves both food intake and waste removal
quiz.why: Cnidarians possess a single opening that functions for both intake and waste removal.

quiz.q: Which order traces increasing body organisation, as the chapter presents it?
quiz.why: Sponges lack tissues, cnidarians add tissues, flatworms add bilateral symmetry.

quiz.q: Which features allow fish to move and breathe in water?
quiz.why: Fins allow movement and gills allow breathing in water.

quiz.q: The correct order of classification ranks is...
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Species, Family, Genus
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Genus, Species

quiz.q: As we move to lower levels of classification, organisms...
quiz.why: At each lower level, organisms share more common features.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter compare classification to a house address?
options: both help locate or identify something exactly, step by step
quiz.why: An address locates a place exactly, just as ranks identify an organism accurately.

quiz.q: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by...
quiz.why: Linnaeus introduced the two-part naming system in the 18th century.

quiz.q: In the name Mangifera indica, the word indica is the...
quiz.why: The first word is the genus; the second, lower-case word is the species.

quiz.q: A scientific name written by hand should be...
quiz.why: Names are italicised in print and underlined when handwritten.

quiz.q: The tiger and lion share the genus Panthera because they...

have the same common name everywhere
were named on the same day

quiz.q: Carl Woese's three domain system was based on...
options: comparisons of DNA, the genetic material
quiz.why: Genetic data showed organisms with similar DNA have a common ancestry.

quiz.q: Fossils are...
options: preserved remains of plants and animals in layers of rocks, sand and mud
kinds of minerals used in industry
quiz.why: The book defines fossils as preserved remains found in layered rocks, sand and mud.

quiz.q: In general, newer rock layers contain...
quiz.why: Older layers hold simpler organisms; newer layers show more complex forms.

examples.title: Sorting plants into their classes
examples.problem: During the monsoon, Ravi finds Spirogyra floating in pond water, and a green mat of Marchantia and moss growing on damp rocks nearby. Using the descriptions in the chapter, name the class of each organism and give one reason for each.
steps: Look at the body of Spirogyra: it is a simple, undifferentiated body called a thallus, which exchanges gases, nutrients and water directly with the surroundings.
Thallophytes are among the simplest plant forms and are mostly found in water or moist environments, so Spirogyra belongs to Thallophyta.
Look at the green mat on the rocks: these plants have root-like rhizoids and simple stem-like and leaf-like structures, and they grow in moist and shady places.
Plants with such bodies that still require water for reproduction are bryophytes, so Marchantia and moss belong to Bryophyta.
examples.answer: Spirogyra is a thallophyte (Thallophyta, algae); Marchantia and moss are bryophytes (Bryophyta).

examples.title: Correcting a scientific name
examples.problem: A student writes the tiger's scientific name as panthera Tigris in her notebook. Using the rules of binomial nomenclature, rewrite it correctly and explain each correction.
steps: Rule one: the name must have two parts, genus and species, so panthera and Tigris must stay together as one name.
Rule two: the genus comes first and begins with a capital letter, so panthera becomes Panthera.
Rule two again: the species name follows in small letters, so Tigris becomes tigris.
Rule three: when handwritten, the scientific name should be underlined.
examples.answer: The correct handwritten form is Panthera tigris, underlined: genus first with a capital letter, species second in lower case.

examples.title: Tracing the tiger through the ranks
examples.problem: Using the hierarchy Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species, explain how the tiger (scientific name Panthera tigris) fits into the classification pyramid shown in Fig. 12.17.
steps: Start at the broadest rank: the tiger belongs to kingdom Animalia, because it is a multicellular, heterotrophic organism.
Move down the ladder: each lower level is a smaller group inside the one above, and organisms there share more common features.
Reach the genus rank: Panthera groups closely related species that share common features, like the roaring cats with similar skull structure, including the lion Panthera leo.
Reach the base: the species tigris marks the group of similar individuals capable of interbreeding and producing offsprings.
examples.answer: The tiger's pyramid runs from kingdom Animalia at the top down to species tigris at the base, with genus Panthera just above it: Panthera tigris.

examples.title: Reading a fossil site like a timeline
examples.problem: A dig in India finds an older rock layer with remains of simple organisms, and a newer layer above it with remains of more complex organisms. What can a scientist conclude from this site, and why?
steps: Identify what was found: fossils, the preserved remains of plants and animals in layers of rocks, sand and mud.
Recall the pattern: generally, older layers contain simpler organisms, while newer layers show more complex forms.
Match the site to the pattern: the older layer with simple remains and the newer layer with complex remains fit exactly.
Draw the conclusion: the site is a natural record showing how life has changed over millions of years.
examples.answer: The site shows life changing over time: simpler organisms in the older layer, more complex forms in the newer layer, exactly as the fossil record predicts.

steps.label: Observe diversity
steps.detail: Life shows endless variety in body form, food habits and habitats.

steps.label: Sort by features
steps.detail: Scientists group organisms by shared features like cell walls, nutrition and body plans.

steps.label: Place in kingdoms
steps.detail: Autotrophic plants with cellulose walls go to Plantae; heterotrophic animals go to Animalia.

steps.label: Zoom into classes
steps.detail: Plantae splits into five classes; Animalia splits by presence or absence of the notochord.

steps.label: Build the hierarchy
steps.detail: Ranks from kingdom to species put every organism into smaller, more specific groups.

steps.label: Name scientifically
steps.detail: Binomial nomenclature gives a two-part genus and species name used worldwide.

steps.label: Check the evidence
steps.detail: Fossils in rock layers record how life has changed over millions of years.

steps.label: Protect biodiversity
steps.detail: Knowing and naming species helps conserve them from pollution, deforestation and climate change.
